title: Workplace Trial: A pick-to-light system in a warehouse
description: Workplace/community source set for the dedicated full mock.
subject: rla
passage:
At Meridian Services, managers and employees were considering a pick-to-light system in a warehouse. Operations director Hana Lee proposed testing light-guided shelf indicators in one packing zone while keeping experienced workers available to verify unusual orders. She argued that the change should begin as a limited trial rather than a permanent rule.

Lee's memo cited three pieces of evidence. the pilot cut average search time by 18 seconds per order, wrong-item picks fell from 2.8 percent to 1.9 percent, and training time for new staff decreased She also separated outcomes that had been measured from benefits that were only expected. For example, the pilot could show whether delays decreased, but it could not prove in advance that employee morale would improve.

Team supervisor Carlos Webb supported testing the idea but raised a concern: the pilot used only common products and may not represent oversized or rarely ordered items. He said a decision affecting the whole organization should not be based only on averages if one department faced a very different workload. He asked that the trial track error rates and overtime as well as speed.

Lee agreed with that addition and responded that the next test should include a mixed-product zone and track correction time as well as initial picking speed. She revised the plan so the trial would include a comparison group, weekly check-ins, and a stop rule if service quality fell below the existing standard for two consecutive weeks.

Employees then debated whether the new safeguards made the proposal too complicated. Some wanted a fast yes-or-no decision. Others argued that a well-designed trial was useful precisely because it could reveal problems before a permanent change. The final plan kept the measurements simple: speed, error rate, overtime, and a short employee survey.

After reviewing the proposal, the leadership team approved the trial but not permanent adoption. The written decision explained that a pilot is evidence-gathering, not proof. A strong recommendation at the end would need to show both that the targeted problem improved and that the change did not simply move costs or errors somewhere less visible.

The situation also shows why workplace decision making cannot be judged from one isolated detail. People in the passage weigh immediate results against longer-term effects, and they revise their choices as new information becomes available.

Another important feature is the way the evidence is limited. The people involved can observe what happened in this setting, but they cannot assume the same outcome would occur everywhere. That distinction matters when readers decide how strongly a conclusion is supported.

The passage repeatedly connects decisions with consequences. Some effects are measured directly, while others are described through observations or testimony. Readers therefore have to separate what the text states from what it only suggests.
